title: Nullable references
sub: string and string? are different promises
cards/0/body:
NullReferenceException is the most common error in .NET. Since C# 8 you can turn on the nullable context: then string means "never null here", and string? means "may be null". The compiler keeps track and warns you.

New projects have it on by default: <Nullable>enable</Nullable>.
cards/1/q: On which line does the compiler warn about a possible null?
cards/1/explain: CS8602: name may be null. Check it, or use name?.Length.
cards/2/body:
Check: if (name is not null) — after that the compiler knows it is not null.
A default value: name ?? "guest".
Last resort: name! — "trust me, it's not null". If you're wrong, you get that very exception.
cards/3/q: What does the ! operator do in name!.Length?
cards/3/options/0: It only silences the warning; nothing is checked at run time
cards/3/options/1: It checks for null and throws a clear exception
cards/3/options/2: It turns null into an empty string
cards/3/explain: It exists only for the compiler.
cards/4/body: A property can't be null, but it is set by an initializer rather than the constructor? required (C# 11) forces you to set it at creation.
cards/5/q: The name, or "guest" if it is null
cards/7/q: Which are true about nullable references? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: It is a compiler check, not a runtime one
cards/7/options/1: They are on by default in new projects
cards/7/options/2: After if (x is not null) the compiler treats x as not null
cards/7/explain: Nullable<T> is only for value types. string? is just an annotation for the compiler.
